analysis.investment_thesis: ACME Solar generates impressive gross margins (99.4%) but every rupee of that margin is largely consumed by INR 759 Cr of annual interest expense — ROCE is a paltry 8.42% and ROE a meagre 7.57%, well below any rational cost of capital. With borrowings surging from INR 8,536 Cr to INR 12,998 Cr in a single year and FCF negative INR 1,719 Cr, this is a capital destruction machine dressed up as a clean-energy story.
key_strengths: Operating margin of 65.28% and gross margin of 99.4% confirm the underlying solar generation economics are sound — sun and PPAs require no raw materials
OCF was positive all 5 years (INR 1,543 Cr in FY25), showing the operational cash generation before financing obligations is genuine
Secured PPAs with central/state government-backed entities provide revenue visibility and lower offtake risk
key_risks: Finance costs of INR 759 Cr nearly equal operating income of INR 1,237 Cr — interest coverage is barely 1.8x and will compress further as debt grows to fund new projects
Borrowings jumped INR 4,462 Cr in a single year (FY25) to INR 12,998 Cr — a company that grows by piling on debt at 8% ROCE is destroying economic value with each new project
Revenue has been declining for 5 years (-4.6% CAGR) even as the solar industry boomed nationally — this suggests structural issues in project mix, tariff erosion, or capacity monetization
red_flags: Net profit of INR 698 Cr in FY24 was almost entirely driven by Other Income of INR 891 Cr — underlying operating profitability is illusory and earnings quality is poor
Promoter holding of 83.29% combined with minimal FII (4.03%) and DII (6.87%) ownership signals that sophisticated institutional investors are largely absent — this is a promoter-controlled story
FCF deeply negative in 3 of last 4 years (-INR 1,719 Cr in FY25) — the company does not generate free cash; it converts equity and debt into long-dated illiquid assets at inadequate returns
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The solar utility business model is straightforward but ACME Solar illustrates why simplicity of operation does not equal investment quality. The economic reality is this: the company earns EBITDA of INR 1,396 Cr but pays INR 759 Cr in interest, leaving very little for equity holders after depreciation and taxes. ROCE of 8.42% barely exceeds the risk-free rate in India — there is no economic value creation happening here. Worse, management is accelerating this value-neutral or value-destructive cycle by borrowing INR 4,462 Cr in a single year to fund new capacity that will likely earn similar single-digit returns.

At 36.8x trailing P/E, the market is pricing ACME Solar as if it is a growth compounder. It is not — revenue has contracted for 5 years, profits are erratic and heavily reliant on non-operating income, and the balance sheet is deteriorating rapidly. The renewable energy sector in India has genuine tailwinds, but owning a highly-leveraged, government-PPA-dependent solar IPP at 37x earnings with 7.6% ROE is not a way to participate in that tailwind — it is a way to finance cheap electricity for the Indian grid at the expense of equity holders. I can find better places to deploy capital.
